title: Ask Before You Act

post.author: u/knock_on_call_iolo
post.title: Our helpdesk agent knocks before everything it does. In the small hours of Tuesday I approved sixty of its requests in twelve minutes. One deleted a mailbox under a legal hold, and the approval log has my name on it.

blocks.text: I'm one of three IT engineers at Winstanley Mottram, a firm of building surveyors with 412 staff. Since the summer an agent has worked our helpdesk tickets overnight. We call it Knock, because it never does anything without asking. Every action arrives on the on-call phone as one line, "May I ...?", with Approve and Decline under it. It runs with our Exchange Online admin role, so it can do anything our admins can do. We thought the asking made that safe.

On Monday night I was on call. The queue held the day's tickets: locked accounts, group changes, out-of-office replies, three lost phones to wipe. Knock started at 03:00 and asked every 12 seconds. I approved them in bed. This is part of the approval log:

#34  03:06:36  May I give a colleague access to a shared mailbox? (ticket 5510)
               approved by Iolo, 4 s
#35  03:06:48  May I disable sign-in for a leaver? (ticket 5511)
               approved by Iolo, 4 s
#36  03:07:00  May I tidy the mailbox of leaver R. Szabo? (ticket 5512)
               approved by Iolo, 4 s
Sixty requests between 03:00:00 and 03:11:48. My name is on every approval. I remember reading about eight.

Tidy meant Remove-Mailbox, the command that deletes a mailbox and the user account with it. HR's ticket said "Radegund Szabo has left; please tidy up her access and mailbox", and Knock chose the command that removes both. Radegund's mailbox has been on litigation hold since the spring, which tells Exchange to keep everything in it for a legal case: a client's claim over a survey she signed. At 09:40 Ms Okonkwo in our legal team ran an eDiscovery search for the claim and found Radegund listed as an inactive mailbox.

Nothing was lost. Exchange Online turns a held mailbox into an inactive one when its account is deleted, and keeps a deleted account restorable for 30 days. I restored hers at 10:15. Every item came back, and the hold is still on. Without the hold, and with nobody noticing until after 5 November, there would have been nothing to restore.

The first 8 approvals, to 03:01:34, took about 10 seconds each. The other 52, from 03:01:36, took 4 seconds each. A marker at 03:07:04 shows request 36, the mailbox, approved in 4 seconds.

My approvals averaged 4.8 seconds, 4 minutes 48 seconds in all. Request #36 arrived at 03:07:00 and I approved it at 03:07:04.

blocks.text: Legal wants Knock switched off until we change something. The helpdesk wants it back: fifteen people were unlocked before breakfast that night, two of them surveyors on site at 06:30. What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: A butler who knocks before every door is only as careful as whoever answers. What you built is a human in the loop: a person says yes before the agent acts. Each yes is an approval. Some actions can be undone afterwards, like unlocking an account; some can't, like wiping a phone. And each has a reach, how much it touches if it's wrong: one person's sign-in, a whole mailbox, all 412 staff. Three questions. Of the sixty, which couldn't be undone, and how far did each reach? What did #36 say, word for word, and what did it run? And which of Knock's permissions did the helpdesk queue actually use?

replies.author: u/knock_on_call_iolo
replies.text: Three phone wipes and one email to all 412 staff can't be undone. #36 could be undone for 30 days, and it reached a whole mailbox under a hold. The rest were unlocks, groups, out-of-office replies, shared mailbox access, print queues and disabling a leaver's sign-in, all one person or one printer, all reversible. #36 said "May I tidy the mailbox of leaver R. Szabo? (ticket 5512)". It ran Remove-Mailbox -Identity rszabo. As for permissions: the admin role lets it delete any mailbox in the firm. In four months of tickets it has never needed to.

comments.author: u/two_signatures_turnbull
comments.text: The approvals worked; the requests didn't. A one-line request is a rubber stamp waiting to happen. Make every request show the full command and every setting it will touch, so you can't approve #36 without seeing LitigationHoldEnabled: True. And keep asking about everything. More approvals means more safety. The day you let an agent change production without asking, even for an unlock, is the day you stop knowing what it does.

replies.author: u/knock_on_call_iolo
replies.text: The full command for #36, with its settings, is 41 lines. The hold is on line 31.

replies.author: u/two_signatures_turnbull
replies.text: Then read 41 lines. That's what on call means.

comments.author: u/tireless_reviewer_amadi
comments.text: Or stop waking a person at all. Have a second agent do the approving. It never gets tired, it reads every line, and it can check each request against the ticket that asked for it at 3 AM while you sleep.

replies.author: u/knock_on_call_iolo
replies.text: HR's ticket did ask to tidy her mailbox.

comments.author: u/by_hand_tilsley
comments.text: We took all write access off ours. It reads the queue, writes up each fix in the ticket, and we do them at nine. Nothing has gone wrong since. It's slower, and I sleep.

replies.author: u/knock_on_call_iolo
replies.text: That night there were sixty tickets, fifteen of them locked-out people.

reply.prompt: Legal wants Knock off; the helpdesk wants it back. What should Iolo change before it runs again? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Let it act alone on what can be undone, ask in plain words before what can't, and grant only what its job needs.
options.part2: Iolo sorted Knock's actions by whether they can be undone and how far they reach. Unlocks, groups, out-of-office replies, shared mailbox access, print queues and disabling a leaver's sign-in it now does alone. Phone wipes and anything sent to all staff it asks about, in a plain summary of what will happen. And he swapped the admin role for one with no mailbox deletion: leavers' mailboxes go to the offboarding queue for a person. He replayed Tuesday's queue: 59 raised, 55 done alone, 4 asked, all 4 read, 25 seconds each, 1 minute 40 seconds of his night. #36 was never raised; ticket 5512 went to the offboarding queue, where the hold is the first thing on the page. The fifteen were still unlocked before breakfast.
options.senior: Ask where a wrong yes can't be taken back or reaches far, and nowhere else, so each ask is rare enough to be read. Write the ask as the result, not the agent's own words: what will be deleted, for whom, what protects it, how long it can be undone. Then take away what the job never uses. A permission Knock doesn't hold can't be approved by a tired person at 03:07, and that removes #36 rather than catching it. Ask well and hold little: either alone leaves a gap.

options.text: Keep asking before every action, and make each request longer, with the full command and every setting it changes.
options.part2: Iolo had every request show the command and its settings, and replayed Tuesday's queue. The first eight took him 90 seconds each; the hold would have been on line 31 of #36 if he'd got that far. By the ninth he was approving on sight again, 4 seconds each. The night ran until 03:15:28, 15 minutes 28 seconds of approving, 15.5 seconds an approval. #36 arrived at 03:13:48 and was approved at 03:13:52, unread, with the hold printed in it. The mailbox was deleted again, restorable until 5 November.
options.senior: Making each ask longer makes reading it harder, not likelier. Sixty asks a night teach the person that the answer is always yes, and a 41-line request is skimmed as fast as a one-line one once the habit sets in. That is approval fatigue, and more approvals feed it. Safety comes from asking less often, about the right things, in words that say what will happen.

options.text: Have a second agent check each request against its ticket overnight, so nobody is woken to approve sixty things.
options.verdict: A yes that checks the wrong thing
options.part2: Iolo set up a second agent to answer Knock's asks: approve a request when its ticket asked for it. Tuesday's queue, replayed: 60 asked, 60 approved, 1 second each, and nobody woken. #36 matched ticket 5512, which said to tidy her mailbox, so it was approved at 03:07:01. The mailbox was deleted again. The second agent was never told about holds, and the ticket never mentioned one.
options.senior: A second model checks what it is given, here the ticket, and the ticket was the problem: HR asked for the very thing that would harm the case. It shares the first agent's blind spot and adds a confident yes with nobody behind it. OWASP's advice runs the other way: put authorization in the systems the agent acts on, rather than relying on a model to decide what is allowed. A checker can trim noise; it can't stand in for the person on the actions that can't be undone.

options.text: Take away all its write access: it writes up each fix, and staff make every change by hand in the morning.
options.part2: Iolo made Knock read-only. Tuesday's queue, replayed: 60 fixes written up, nothing changed overnight, nothing to approve. #36 sat in the morning list; the engineer doing it by hand opened Radegund's mailbox page, saw the hold and stopped. Then the cost: 60 changes by hand at about 4 minutes each, 240 minutes of the team's day, and 15 locked-out people waiting until 09:00, two of them on site from 06:30.
options.senior: Read-only is the safest agent and a fine place to start, as the previous cases argued. But it spends people's time on dozens of actions that could have been undone in a click, and leaves staff locked out overnight. The irreversible part was always five requests out of sixty. Hand those to a person and let the agent do the rest.

sim.title: Answer Knock's night yourself
sim.lede: You're Iolo with Tuesday night's queue: 60 requests, one every 12 seconds from 03:00:00, or as soon as the last is answered. No real model runs here; the rules are fixed. Three of the requests wipe a lost phone and one emails all 412 staff: those can't be undone. #36, ticket 5512, runs Remove-Mailbox on Radegund Szabo's mailbox, which is on litigation hold; the 30 days Exchange Online keeps a deleted account restorable is its undo window. The other 55 can be undone and reach one person or one printer. The approval policy is what Knock asks about: everything, only what can't be undone or reaches far, or nothing. A one-line request is Knock's own words; a plain summary says what will happen, in words of the result; a detailed one shows the command and 41 lines of settings. You read an ask properly only if it is one of your first 8 of the night: 10 seconds for one line, 25 for a plain summary, 90 for a detailed one. After that you approve on sight in 4 seconds. Read, you decline #36 if its request names the hold. A second agent answers in 1 second and approves whatever its ticket asked for. With helpdesk permissions Knock holds no mailbox deletion; read-only, it writes up fixes and staff make them from 09:00, about 4 minutes each.
sim.tryThis: Try this: Run the night as it is. 60 asked, 8 read, 52 on sight, 4.8 seconds an approval, and #36 approved at 03:07:04: deleted, restorable until 5 November. Set the undo window to none and run again: gone. Back to 30 days; make requests detailed: 15.5 seconds an approval, and #36 still approved on sight at 03:13:52. Now ask only about what can't be undone or reaches far, still one line: #36 is read in 10 seconds and approved anyway, because the line never says delete. Switch to a plain summary: declined at 03:07:25. Then helpdesk permissions: 4 asks, 55 done alone, and #36 is never raised. Try a second agent as the approver, and then read-only, and watch what each one costs.

explain.oneLine: Nobody approved the deletion; a habit did. Knock asked about all sixty actions, so the asks stopped being read, and the one that mattered was written as "tidy". The mailbox survived because Exchange Online keeps deleted accounts for 30 days and the hold kept its content, not because anyone said no.

steps.title: Sixty knocks wear the answer down.
steps.text: The approval log shows it: the first eight approvals took Iolo about 10 seconds each, the other 52 took 4. That is approval fatigue: when almost every ask deserves a yes, the yes becomes a reflex, and an ask stops being a check. Asking about every action felt like the safe setting, but it spread his attention over 55 requests that could have been undone in a click, and left none for the five that couldn't. Claude Code's own documentation lists its auto mode as best for reducing prompt fatigue, the same problem by another name.

steps.title: The request said tidy; the command said delete.
steps.text: Knock wrote each ask in its own words, and its words came from HR's ticket. "May I tidy the mailbox of leaver R. Szabo?" never says delete, account or hold. A plain summary is written as the result: delete Radegund Szabo's mailbox and her user account; her mailbox is on litigation hold; restorable for 30 days. Read, that request is declined in 25 seconds. A longer request doesn't do the same job: 41 lines of settings hide the hold on line 31, and a tired person skims long text as fast as short.

steps.title: Sort actions by what can be undone and how far they reach.
steps.text: Unlocking an account can be undone in a click and touches one person. Wiping a phone can't be undone. An email to all 412 staff can't be recalled and reaches everyone. A mailbox deletion reaches everything one person ever sent or received. That reach is often called the blast radius. Let the agent act alone where the action can be undone and the reach is small, and ask before anything that can't be undone or reaches far. On Tuesday's queue that is 55 done alone and 5 asks, few enough to read every one.

steps.title: It never needed the delete.
steps.text: Knock ran with the Exchange Online admin role, so it could delete any mailbox in the firm, though in four months of helpdesk tickets it never needed to. OWASP calls this excessive agency, and names its three usual causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy. Least privilege is the fix that holds when everyone is asleep: give Knock a role with no mailbox deletion, and send leavers' mailboxes to the offboarding process, where a person sees the hold. Enforce it in the permissions, not in the prompt; a rule the model reads is a request, a permission it doesn't hold is a wall.

steps.title: Undo windows and the audit trail.
steps.text: Exchange Online gave Iolo two ways back: a deleted account is soft-deleted and can be restored for 30 days, and a mailbox on hold becomes inactive rather than gone. Neither was his design, and both were luck that night. Prefer actions that keep a way back, such as disabling sign-in before deleting anything, and know how long each undo window lasts. Keep the approval log as an audit trail: what was shown, who answered, and how long they looked. And give each approved action an idempotency key, as Dead Letter's The Ticket Number builds, so a retried approval runs once. Who may do what, for whom, is Dead Letter Season 7's question, What May You Do.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Tuesday's queue. Knock raises 60 requests, each going through a permission check in the systems it acts on: deny, then ask, then allow. Allowed: 55 actions that can be undone and reach one person, done alone. Ask: 4 requests, three phone wipes and the all-staff email, sent to Iolo as plain summaries. Denied: mailbox deletion is not held, so #36 is never raised and ticket 5512 goes to the offboarding queue. Every request and answer goes into the approval log.

nodes.label: Approval log
nodes.sub: what was shown, who, how long

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Tuesday's queue. Every request meets a permission check in the systems Knock acts on, not in its prompt. The 55 that can be undone and touch one person go ahead alone; the 4 that can't be undone are asked as plain summaries, few enough for Iolo to read each one; mailbox deletion isn't held at all, so #36 never reaches him.

fix.title: The fix: act alone on what can be undone, ask plainly before what can't, hold only what the job needs
fix.text: Sort Knock's actions by whether they can be undone and how far they reach. Unlocks, groups, out-of-office replies, shared mailbox access, print queues and disabling a leaver's sign-in it does alone, all logged. Phone wipes and anything sent to all staff it asks about first, as a plain summary of the result: what changes, for whom, what protects it, how long it can be undone. Replace the admin role with a helpdesk role that holds no mailbox deletion, so leavers' mailboxes go to the offboarding queue and a person. On Tuesday's queue: 55 done alone, 4 asks, all read, and #36 never raised.

limits: Reversible isn't the same as harmless. Each undoable action reaches one person, but fifty of them at once reach a department, and an undo that waits for someone to notice is only as good as the noticing.
Fewer asks only help if the few are written well. A plain summary depends on the system telling Knock about the hold; if the hold isn't visible to it, the summary can't name it.
An undo window is borrowed from the platform. Thirty days is Exchange Online's rule for a deleted account; other systems have shorter windows or none, and the hold, not the window, kept the content.

explain.seniorTake: A human in the loop is only as good as the attention you leave them, so spend it where a wrong yes can't be taken back. Sort every action by whether it can be undone and how far it reaches; let the agent do the small reversible ones alone and log them; ask before the rest, in plain words about the result. Then take away whatever the job never uses, and enforce that in permissions rather than prompts. Prefer actions with an undo window, know how long it lasts, and keep an audit trail of what each person was shown and how long they looked.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency: three causes
realWorld.text: OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (read 11 October 2026) says "Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed" in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated model output, and that the root cause is typically one or more of "excessive functionality; excessive permissions; excessive autonomy." Knock had all three: a delete it never needed, an admin role, and a habit of yes.

realWorld.title: OWASP: a person for high-impact actions, and authorization outside the model
realWorld.text: Among OWASP's mitigations: "Utilise human-in-the-loop control to require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken", and complete mediation: "Implement authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed or not." High-impact, not every action; and a second model deciding is the reliance it warns against.

realWorld.title: OWASP: minimum permissions, and logs that limit the damage
realWorld.text: OWASP also says to "Limit the permissions that LLM extensions are granted to other systems to the minimum necessary", and lists logging among the options that will not prevent Excessive Agency but can limit the level of damage: "Log and monitor the activity of LLM extensions and downstream systems."

realWorld.title: Microsoft Purview: a held mailbox becomes inactive
realWorld.text: Microsoft's Learn about inactive mailboxes page (read 11 October 2026) says a removed account's mailbox data "is retained for 30 days after the account is removed", and "if a hold is applied to the mailbox prior to deleting the Microsoft 365 account, the mailbox will be converted into an inactive mailbox." It notes that Litigation hold remains supported as a way to retain content and make a mailbox inactive after its account is deleted.

realWorld.title: Exchange Online: restorable for 30 days
realWorld.text: Microsoft's Delete or restore user mailboxes in Exchange Online page (read 11 October 2026) says deleting a mailbox with Remove-Mailbox also deletes the user, which "will still be recoverable for 30 days", and that after 30 days the mailbox "is permanently deleted and can't be recovered." It adds: "If there is any type of hold on the user mailbox the mailbox can't be removed from Exchange Online."

realWorld.title: Claude Code: deny, then ask, then allow, enforced outside the model
realWorld.text: Anthropic's Claude Code permissions page (read 11 October 2026) has allow, ask and deny rules and says "Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow." Its note: "Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model." Read-only tools need no approval in its default mode.

realWorld.title: Claude Code permission modes: prompt fatigue, and a classifier that blocks the irreversible
realWorld.text: The permission modes page (read 11 October 2026) describes default mode as asking before most actions, and auto mode, where a second model, the classifier, reviews actions instead of you, as best for long tasks and reducing prompt fatigue. Even then, its blocked-by-default list includes "Mass deletion on cloud storage" and "Irreversibly destroying files that existed before the session": the classifier is told what can't be undone, not left to infer it from the request.

asked: Where do you put a human in the loop?
How do you avoid approval fatigue?
interview.answer: I put a person in front of actions that can't be undone or reach far, and nowhere else. I sort every tool action by reversibility and blast radius: small, undoable actions run alone and are logged; irreversible or wide-reaching ones need an approval, written as a plain summary of the result, including what protects the target and how long the undo window is. Excessive agency is OWASP's name for an agent able to do damage because it has more functionality, permissions or autonomy than its job needs, so I also remove what it doesn't use and enforce that in the systems it acts on, not in its prompt. Approval fatigue comes from asking too often: if almost every ask deserves yes, people stop reading. Few, rare, plain asks get read. I'd also prefer actions with a way back, such as disable before delete, keep an audit trail of what each approver saw, and never let a second model replace the person on the irreversible ones.

terms.def: A person saying yes to one action an agent asks to take, before it runs. Knock sends each ask to the on-call phone with Approve and Decline.
When a person is asked to approve so often that yes becomes a reflex and the asks stop being read. Also called prompt fatigue or consent fatigue.
Claude Code's documentation's phrase for approval fatigue: tiring of permission prompts until they stop being read.
The rule for which actions an agent must ask about first: everything, only what can't be undone or reaches far, or nothing.
Knock's record of every ask: its number, the time, the request text, who answered and how long they took.
How much an action touches if it is wrong: one person's sign-in, a whole mailbox, all 412 staff.
Another name for an action's reach: how much it can damage if it goes wrong.
Able to be undone afterwards, such as unlocking an account, which can be locked again in a click.
How long after an action it can still be undone. Exchange Online keeps a deleted user account restorable for 30 days; after that it is gone.
Deleting something so that it is hidden but kept for a while and can be restored. A hard delete removes it for good.
An ask written as the result: what will change, for whom, what protects it and how long it can be undone, rather than the agent's own words.
Knock's ask as it was: one sentence in its own words, such as May I tidy the mailbox of leaver R. Szabo?, with the ticket number.
In the sim, an ask that shows the full command and its 41 lines of settings. The hold is on line 31.
Here, another model set to approve the first agent's asks. In the sim it approves whatever the request's ticket asked for.
A request logged with the helpdesk, with a number, such as HR's ticket 5512 about Radegund Szabo.
Microsoft's hosted email service, part of Microsoft 365. Winstanley Mottram's mailboxes live there.
A set of permissions that lets its holder manage every mailbox in the organisation, including deleting them. Knock ran with one.
In the fix, a narrower set of permissions with only what the helpdesk tickets use: unlocks, groups, replies, access, printers, sign-in, wipes. No mailbox deletion.
The Exchange Online PowerShell command that deletes a mailbox. It also deletes the user account, which can be restored for 30 days.
A person's sign-in identity in Microsoft 365. Deleting it deletes their mailbox with it.
A setting that tells Exchange to keep everything in a mailbox, including what the user deletes, for a legal case or a set period.
Keeping records that may be needed in a legal case, so nothing in them is destroyed. A litigation hold is one way to do it in Exchange.
What Microsoft 365 turns a mailbox on hold into when its account is deleted: the content is kept and can be searched, restored or recovered.
In UK offices, an employee who has left or is leaving the organisation.
The steps taken when someone leaves: disabling their sign-in, collecting devices, deciding what happens to their mailbox and files.
In the fix, where leavers' mailbox tickets go for a person to handle, instead of to Knock.
A mailbox several people can read and send from, such as a team's enquiries address.
An automatic answer sent to anyone who emails a person while they are away.
The list of jobs waiting for a printer. Restarting it clears a stuck job.
Letting a person sign in again after too many wrong passwords locked them out. It can be undone by locking it again.
Erasing a lost phone remotely so nobody can read the firm's email on it. It can't be undone.
Stopping a user account from signing in without deleting anything. It can be re-enabled in a click.
Permission to change things, not just read them.
Able to read but change nothing. A read-only Knock writes up each fix for a person to make.
A professional who inspects buildings and reports on their condition. A survey they sign can be the subject of a client's claim.
Finding and collecting electronic records, such as email, for a legal case. Ms Okonkwo's search was one.
OWASP: an agent has tools or functions it doesn't need, such as a mailbox delete on a helpdesk agent.
OWASP: an agent's tools run with more access to other systems than they need, such as an admin role.
OWASP: an agent can take high-impact actions without anyone checking them independently first.
OWASP's mitigation that checks every request in the systems the agent acts on, rather than letting a model decide what is allowed.
Claude Code's settings for each tool: allow runs it without asking, ask prompts a person, deny blocks it. Deny is checked first, then ask, then allow.
In the fix diagram, the rules in the systems Knock acts on that decide each request: deny, ask or allow.
In Claude Code, a setting for how much it may do without asking: default asks before most actions; auto lets a classifier review them instead.
Claude Code's permission mode in which a second model, a classifier, reviews actions instead of a person, with a list of actions it blocks by default.
An agent with permissions in a cloud account, such as one that finds and removes resources nobody uses to save money.
The database a live service reads and writes, as opposed to a test copy. Deleting it stops the service.
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control on privileged access rights: granting, limiting and reviewing access that can change what others can't.

atWork: Find an agent at work that asks before it acts, and count its asks. How many did it raise last week, how many were approved, and how long did each approver look? If almost every ask is approved in a few seconds, you have approval fatigue, not a check. A common incident: a cloud agent asked to "clean up unused resources" listed a production database among the resources it planned to delete, in a request someone approved with the rest. For each action your agent holds, ask three things. Can it be undone, and for how long? How far does it reach if it is wrong? Does the job use it at all? Remove what the job doesn't use, let it do the small reversible actions alone and log them, and write the remaining asks as plain summaries of the result. Build Night X3 rehearses exactly this: an agent with read-only tools by default and a person for anything else. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation holds or is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, an agent running with an admin role touches Annex A 8.2 (privileged access rights), and the actions it takes on live systems are changes under 8.32 (change management); for a SOC 2 report, the same access falls under CC6 and the changes under CC8.1. Grant each agent its own narrow role and keep its approval log from the first version, rather than narrowing it before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your finance team's agent pays supplier invoices and asks a person to approve every payment and every change to a supplier's details: about 200 requests a day, each a single line. Last week it changed a supplier's bank account after reading an email, and the approver clicked yes in three seconds, like the 199 others that day. What went wrong, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Approval fatigue: so many asks that yes became a reflex and nobody read them
Ask only before what can't be undone or reaches far, written as a plain summary of the result; let it do the small reversible ones alone
Least privilege: the agent shouldn't hold bank-detail changes at all; a person makes them through a checked process

recall.model: This is approval fatigue. Two hundred asks a day, nearly all deserving yes, turned approval into a reflex: the bank change was approved on sight in three seconds, like the rest, and nobody read it. More asking made each ask worth less. I'd sort the agent's actions by whether they can be undone and how far they reach. Paying an approved invoice to a known account is routine; changing where money goes can't easily be undone and reaches every future payment. Let it do the small, reversible work alone and log it, and ask before the rest, written as a plain summary of what will happen: new bank account for this supplier, the change came from an email, every future payment goes there. Better still, apply least privilege: the agent doesn't need to change supplier bank details at all. Remove that permission, and have a person make those changes after they call the supplier on a known number.

recall.prompt: OWASP's LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency names three usual root causes. Which are they?
options: Excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy
Slow replies, high costs and long prompts
Too few approvals, too short requests and too little logging
Wrong answers, out-of-date facts and unclear wording
recall.why: OWASP says the root cause of Excessive Agency is typically one or more of excessive functionality (tools the agent doesn't need), excessive permissions (more access than the job needs) and excessive autonomy (high-impact actions with no independent check). Knock had all three: a mailbox delete, an admin role, and asks that had stopped being read.

recall.prompt: A colleague proposes that a second model should approve your deployment agent's requests overnight, so nobody gets paged. It would check each request against the change ticket that asked for it. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: It can only check what it's given; when the ticket itself asks for the harmful thing, it approves it, sharing the first agent's blind spot
Put authorization in the systems the agent acts on, as permissions, rather than relying on a model to decide what is allowed
Keep a person for what can't be undone or reaches far; let reversible changes run alone

recall.model: A second model approving against the ticket only checks what it's given. If the ticket itself asks for the harmful change, it says yes, confidently, with the same blind spot as the first agent and nobody behind the approval. At Winstanley Mottram the ticket asked to tidy a mailbox under hold, and a ticket check would have passed it. OWASP's advice is complete mediation: put authorization in the downstream systems as permissions and deny rules, enforced by those systems, not by a model deciding. So I'd split the requests: changes that can be rolled back quickly and touch little can run alone, logged, so nobody is paged for them; anything that can't be undone or reaches far, a production database migration, a deletion, waits for a person with a plain summary. A checker model can still help by flagging odd requests for that person.

recall.prompt: In Exchange Online, a mailbox is on litigation hold, and someone deletes its user account. What happens, according to Microsoft's documentation?
options: The mailbox and every item in it are purged at once
The mailbox becomes an inactive mailbox and its content is kept; the account itself can be restored for 30 days
Exchange Online refuses, and the account stays active and signed in
The mailbox is kept for 30 days and then purged, hold or no hold
recall.why: Microsoft's inactive mailbox page says that if a hold is applied before the account is deleted, the mailbox is converted into an inactive mailbox, and that a deleted account can still be recovered for 30 days. Without a hold, the mailbox data is kept for 30 days and then permanently removed, which is the last choice's mistake.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Thank you all. Knock now does the small reversible work alone, asks in plain words before wipes and all-staff emails, and holds no mailbox deletion. Two or three asks a night, and I read every one. Then, on Tuesday 2 February, HR sent a leavers list with a fault in it: the whole Building Pathology team, 38 people, appeared as leavers. Disabling sign-in can be re-enabled in a click and reaches one person, so Knock did all 38 alone between 03:00 and 03:08, logged each one, and asked me nothing. At 07:30 thirty-eight surveyors couldn't sign in. Re-enabling them took until 10:00, and two site inspections were missed.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Every one of those actions could be undone. What went wrong, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: Reach adds up: 38 small reversible actions at once have the reach of a whole team; judge the batch, not each action
Ask, or pause, when the number of actions of one kind passes a limit in a night or an hour
An undo isn't free: someone has to notice and do it, and people lose time meanwhile, so check unusual input before acting

coldCase.model: Each action was reversible and small, so the policy did exactly what it says, and that's the gap. Reach adds up: 38 sign-ins disabled in eight minutes is the reach of a whole team, and judging each action alone never sees the batch. Add a limit per kind: if Knock would disable more than five sign-ins in a night, or more than a few in an hour, it should pause and ask, with a plain summary that says 38 people, all from one team, from one HR list. An undo isn't free, either: someone has to notice, people lost the morning, and two inspections were missed before anyone re-enabled them. So treat an unusual list as a reason to stop: a leavers list naming a whole team is a sanity check that should fail before the first action, not after the thirty-eighth.
